record.paper_title: Open questions on defining and computing the vapour-liquid surface tension by virial and test transformation approaches
record.context_brief: Laplace surface tension as free-energy derivative
record.original_question: How, if at all, can the Laplace surface tension γ_L = σ_L of a spherical vapour-liquid interface be expressed as a free-energy derivative? The obstruction is that the familiar derivative γ = (∂F/∂a) at fixed particle number N, volume V, and temperature T is rigorous for planar interfaces but becomes problematic for spherical interfaces because N, V, and T determine the area; in the thermodynamic variables developed for spherical dividing surfaces, the analogous derivative gives zero where a surface tension γ is expected.

evidence.quote: this, again, can be formulated stringently in the planar case, where we may writeF (N, V, T, a) for the two-phase system, and the four arguments are independent thermodynamic degrees of freedom. In the spherical case,N, V, andT determine a, and the above to some extent becomes an abuse of notation – it suggests a stronger basis of the method in thermodynamics than it actually has.
However, it becomes (∂F/∂aν)N,V,T = γν − Rν∆P/2 = 0; Sampayo et al.[1] explicitly require this to beγ, not zero.

First, it is not clear how we should express the Laplace surface tension as a free energy derivative. Since σL = γL, this could be done from any of the expressions for σν or for γν, but the development from Section 4 does not provide us with an obvious starting point. Instead, we found that Eq. (17) doesnot work within the system of variables developed here – we obtained a zero where we should have obtainedγ according to Sampayoet al. [1].

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a two-phase vapour–liquid system in thermodynamic equilibrium with a single spherical liquid drop (or vapour bubble) of radius R immersed in the coexisting bulk phase, at temperature T, with total particle number N and total volume V. Let F(N,V,T) denote the Helmholtz free energy of the system. For each choice of a Gibbs dividing surface of radius R_ν with area a_ν = 4πR_ν² and corresponding surface tension γ_ν, the Laplace pressure jump across the interface is ΔP = P_liq − P_vap, and the surface of tension R_s is characterized by the Young–Laplace relation ΔP = 2γ_s/R_s; for a general dividing surface one has γ_ν = γ_s + (R_ν − R_s) ΔP/… (the standard Gibbs–Tolman relations). Define the Laplace surface tension γ_L = σ_L as the value γ_s appearing in the mechanical Young–Laplace law.

For a planar vapour–liquid interface, one can introduce the area a as an independent thermodynamic variable and the surface tension is rigorously given by γ = (∂F/∂a)_{N,V,T}. For a spherical interface, however, N, V and T already determine the equilibrium radius and hence the area a, so this derivative formula is not directly meaningful; furthermore, working in a system of thermodynamic variables in which area is treated as an additional coordinate produces (∂F/∂a_ν)_{N,V,T} = γ_ν − R_ν ΔP/2, which vanishes identically on the equimolar (or other natural) dividing surface conventions, rather than giving γ.

Problem. Provide a rigorous thermodynamic construction expressing the Laplace surface tension γ_L of a spherical vapour–liquid interface as a partial derivative of an appropriate (free) energy with respect to a suitably defined area-like variable, with all other variables held fixed, in such a way that:
(i) the construction reduces to γ = (∂F/∂a)_{N,V,T} in the planar limit R → ∞;
(ii) the resulting derivative equals γ_L (equivalently γ_s) on the surface of tension and not zero;
(iii) the choice of independent thermodynamic variables and constraints used is internally consistent for a finite spherical interface.
Alternatively, prove that no such free-energy derivative representation of γ_L exists.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is explicitly posed as an open conceptual problem in the literature on vapour–liquid surface tension for curved interfaces. Standard references give γ = (∂G/∂A) at constant T,P,n for gently curved interfaces, but no consistent free-energy derivative formulation for the Laplace surface tension of a spherical interface, satisfying the planar limit and giving γ rather than zero, appears to be established. No published resolution was located.

status_evidence.title: Surface tension - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Surface tension can be expressed as a partial derivative of the Gibbs free energy with respect to the surface area at constant T,P,n.
status_evidence.claim: Standard definition is valid for planar/gently curved interfaces but does not straightforwardly extend to finite spherical interfaces.

status_evidence.title: Numerical approaches to determine the interface tension of curved interfaces from free energy calculations
status_evidence.snippet: Free energy calculations for curved interface tensions remain a subject of active methodological development.
status_evidence.claim: Determining curved-interface tension from free-energy considerations is still an active research area.

status_evidence.title: Open questions on defining and computing the vapour-liquid surface tension
status_evidence.snippet: It is not clear how we should express the Laplace surface tension as a free energy derivative.
status_evidence.claim: The problem is stated as open.
